title: With the Photographer
author: Stephen Leacock
tagline: A comic clash between a man who wants a true likeness and a photographer who treats his face as a mistake to be corrected.

sourceNote.thirdParty: "With the Photographer" is a humorous prose sketch by Stephen Leacock (first collected in Behind the Beyond, 1913) and remains the property of its copyright holder. It is not reproduced here. Read the sketch in your prescribed textbook.

overview.intro: A man visits a photographer to have his portrait taken and discovers that the photographer regards his face as a problem to be solved. What begins as a comic lesson in posture becomes a quiet argument about identity: should a photograph capture the face you actually have, or the face an expert thinks you should have? Leacock tells the whole story through the narrator's own voice, so the humour and the hurt arrive together.

learn.title: Before you read: the world of the sketch

blocks.text: Stephen Leacock wrote for readers who knew the small embarrassances of modern city life: shops, services and experts who explained to ordinary people how they were doing everything wrong. Photography in the early twentieth century was still a formal occasion — you dressed up, sat still, and waited for a professional to decide whether you had done it correctly. Leacock takes that ordinary errand and pushes it to its logical extreme, so that a routine portrait session becomes a trial of the narrator's own face.

As you read, notice that we never learn the narrator's name and never see the photograph itself. Everything reaches us through his retelling, months or years later, in a tone that is still half-embarrassed. That distance is part of the comedy: he is gentle enough to mock himself, but honest enough to admit that the experience stung.

The narrator arrives for his sitting in good spirits, only to be told that his face is 'quite wrong'. The photographer takes charge: he turns the narrator's head, corrects his posture, and arranges his features as if assembling a face from spare parts. The picture is taken while the narrator is still protesting. When he returns for the proof, the photograph has been retouched — the eyes altered, the eyebrows removed, the mouth adjusted — and the photographer now proposes to repair the ears as well.

items: The visit begins as a transaction: the narrator is the customer, and he expects a service.
The photographer reverses the roles: the narrator becomes the raw material, and the photographer is the authority who judges it.
At the second visit the 'corrections' have gone further than any of the agreed work — the proof no longer records a face, it records an opinion.
The narrator asks for his own likeness, is refused in effect, tells the photographer to keep the picture, and leaves in tears.
The ending turns comedy into a small, genuine grief: he was not laughed at for his face, he was laughed at for having it.

items.text: The narrator accepts criticism politely for several paragraphs before objecting at all.
items.note: Leacock's comic method: the narrator's good manners make the photographer's presumption funnier and the final hurt sharper.

items.text: The photographer proposes to alter the ears, a part of the face no one had complained about.
items.note: Each new 'improvement' widens the gap between what was asked for (a portrait) and what is being delivered (a redesign).

blocks.text: There are only two people in the sketch, and Leacock defines them entirely through what they say and do. The narrator is self-conscious but quick-witted; he can describe his own humiliation in a way that makes a reader smile, yet his final tears show that the wound was real. He never becomes angry or abusive — his protest is always phrased as a reasonable request for the thing he paid for: a picture of himself.

The photographer is polite, absorbed and immovable. He never argues with the narrator; he simply continues working, because in his professional world a face is a set of correctable faults. He has no name and no face of his own in the narrative, which is fitting: in this studio, only the customer's appearance is under discussion. The comedy depends on the mismatch between the two men — one wants a memory, the other wants a result.

items.meaning: The unnamed first-person teller of the sketch, whose voice supplies all the humour and all the sympathy.
The unnamed professional who treats the narrator's face as material to be improved.
A faithful resemblance — the thing the narrator asks for and never receives.
To alter a photograph by hand; here it becomes a metaphor for refusing to accept people as they are.

blocks.text: The sketch satirises the modern idea that every natural feature is a correctable defect. The photographer's studio is a small kingdom of expertise where the customer's wishes matter less than the expert's standards; Leacock had written elsewhere about exactly this species of authority, from doctors to dentists to professors. The narrator's polite, increasingly helpless objections voice the ordinary person's position: he cannot argue with a professional about what a face should look like.

Underneath the satire lies the theme of self-acceptance. The narrator does not want to be made beautiful; he wants to recognise himself. When the photograph is changed beyond recognition, what is lost is not attractiveness but truth — and the tears at the end show that the loss is personal, not practical. A reader is meant to laugh at the situation and then notice, a beat later, that the joke is about how quickly we are told to dislike our own faces.

items: Appearance versus authenticity: a portrait should record, not flatter.
Expert authority: the professional's opinion overrules the customer's request.
Conformity and 'improvement': every feature is measured against an imagined ideal.
Identity: to have your likeness erased is to be told you are a mistake.
Comedy and pain together: Leacock's narrator is funny precisely because he is hurt.

blocks.text: Leacock's humour works by understatement and escalation. The narrator describes outrageous interference in perfectly reasonable sentences, and each visit escalates the previous one: first the posture is corrected, then the features, then the finished picture. The prose stays calm while the situation grows absurd, and the gap between the polite tone and the humiliating content is where the comedy lives.

items: Because the narrator is unnamed, he stands in for any reader who has been told to improve themselves.
The absent photograph lets each reader imagine the worst 'improvement' of their own face.
Dialogue is used sparingly: the photographer mostly speaks in pronouncements, never explanations.

learn.title: Reading and writing tips for this sketch

blocks.text: In an examination, answers about this sketch should always be anchored in the narrator's voice: quote the polite phrasing, describe what changes between the two visits, and end with the effect of the final tears. Avoid retelling the plot at length — examiners look for the method (how Leacock makes it funny) and the meaning (what the funniness criticises). Practise writing one paragraph that explains why a 'comic' sketch can still be a serious one.

items: Structure a character answer around: what the narrator wants, what the photographer does, and how the narrator reacts.
For a theme answer, contrast 'being seen' with 'being improved' as the sketch's two positions.
When asked about humour, name the technique (understatement, escalation, repetition) before illustrating it.
The ending is the favourite examination target: be ready to explain in two sentences why the tears matter.

keyPoints: The sketch is told in the first person by an unnamed narrator, so all comedy and all sympathy come through his own voice.
The central conflict is between a likeness (truth) and an improvement (an expert's ideal).
Leacock builds humour by escalation: posture first, then eyes, eyebrows and mouth, then the ears.
The tone stays polite and understated while the situation becomes absurd — that gap is the comedy.
The photographer is never explained or argued with; he simply works, which makes him a symbol of unanswerable expertise.
The photograph itself never appears, which lets every reader picture their own 'corrected' face.
The tears at the end turn a funny sketch into a small tragedy of self-acceptance.
Because the story is retrospective, the narrator is laughing at his past self — and still quietly upset with the photographer.
examFocus: Character question: describe the narrator as self-conscious but witty, and the photographer as polite, absorbed and immovable — then illustrate each from the two visits.
Humour question: always name the technique (escalation, understatement, repetition) before you quote or paraphrase an incident.
Theme question: the sketch opposes acceptance of the self against expert-approved 'improvement'; the ending proves which side the narrator takes.
Style question: explain why Leacock keeps the narrator unnamed and the photograph unseen.
The final tears are a recurring examination target — practise a two-sentence answer on why they matter.
Do not retell at length: a strong answer devotes most of its space to method and meaning, not plot.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator visit the photographer?
options: To have his portrait taken and receive a true likeness of himself
To apply for a job as the photographer's assistant
To complain about a photograph taken by a rival studio
To buy a camera for his own use at home
questions.answer: To have his portrait taken and receive a true likeness of himself
questions.explanation: The narrator comes as a customer: he wants a picture of his own face. Every later argument in the sketch follows from that simple request, which the photographer quietly replaces with his own idea of how the face should look.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing an option that mentions complaining — the narrator objects only after the proof is altered, and even then politely.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator do when he sees the retouched proof?
options: He praises the photographer's skill and pays for extra copies
He asks the photographer to restore his original appearance in the picture
He tells the photographer to keep the picture and leaves in tears
He demands that the photographer erase the photograph in his presence
questions.answer: He tells the photographer to keep the picture and leaves in tears
questions.explanation: Faced with a photograph that no longer resembles him — eyes retouched, eyebrows removed, mouth adjusted — the narrator abandons his claim to the picture, tells the photographer to keep it, and walks out weeping. The comic sketch ends on genuine hurt.
questions.commonMistake: Softening the ending: the tears are explicit, and they are what give the sketch its seriousness.

questions.prompt: How does the photographer treat the narrator during the sitting? Give two details.
questions.answer: The photographer treats the narrator as material to be arranged rather than as a customer: he turns the narrator's head and corrects his posture to suit himself, and he takes the picture while the narrator is still objecting. He judges the face itself 'quite wrong', as though it were a defect in his workshop rather than a person's appearance.
questions.explanation: Two clear details are wanted: physical control (turning the head, fixing the posture) and professional dismissal (declaring the face wrong, shooting over the protest). Together they show the reversal of roles — the paying customer is being handled like an object.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the second visit instead: the question asks about the sitting itself.

questions.prompt: What changes in the photograph between the sitting and the proof?
questions.answer: When the narrator returns for the proof, the photographer has retouched the eyes, removed the eyebrows and adjusted the mouth — and he now proposes altering the ears as well. The proof therefore records the photographer's opinions about faces rather than the narrator's actual appearance.
questions.explanation: The alterations widen from visit to visit: what began as instructions about posture has become a list of edits to the finished image, ending with a plan to change a feature nobody had criticised.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only one alteration — the answer should show the pattern of escalating interference.

questions.prompt: Explain how Leacock creates humour in this sketch. Refer to at least two techniques in your answer.
questions.answer: Leacock builds humour through escalation and understatement. Escalation: the photographer first corrects the narrator's posture, then his features, then the finished photograph itself, and finally proposes to fix the ears — each 'improvement' is more absurd than the last, yet presented as routine work. Understatement: the narrator reacts to outrageous interference with polite, reasonable sentences instead of outrage, so the gap between the calm tone and the humiliating content makes the reader laugh. A third device is perspective: told in retrospect by the narrator himself, the sketch lets him mock his own submission even while admitting it hurt.
questions.explanation: A strong humour answer names the technique, illustrates it with a specific moment, and explains the effect. Escalation supplies the structure of the comedy; understatement supplies its tone; the first-person retrospection supplies its self-mockery.
questions.commonMistake: Merely retelling funny incidents without naming how the humour is produced — technique must come first.

questions.prompt: What is Leacock satirising in the figure of the photographer? Illustrate your answer.
questions.answer: Leacock satirises the authority of the expert over the ordinary person. The photographer never explains his judgements or defends them; he simply announces that the face is wrong and works on it, because professional opinion in his world outranks the customer's wishes. His studio becomes a small kingdom where the person being served has no say — the narrator pays, yet cannot get the one thing he asked for. The satire is aimed not at one rude man but at a modern habit: the belief that professionals may redefine what is normal, right down to the shape of a face.
questions.explanation: The answer must move from the character to the general target: the photographer's unargued pronouncements and unasked-for alterations show expertise overriding consent, which is what Leacock is criticising.
questions.commonMistake: Criticising only the photographer as an individual and stopping there — satire questions require the wider human target.

questions.prompt: Why does the sketch end with the narrator in tears? What does the ending suggest about him?
questions.answer: The tears show that the narrator's distress is deeper than the comic situation suggests. He came to be seen as he is, and instead was told — repeatedly, professionally, cheerfully — that his real face was a mistake to be corrected. His plea to be photographed as himself was ignored, so the altered proof becomes a small symbol of being misunderstood by people in authority. Ending on tears rather than anger suggests that he is gentle and self-aware rather than combative: he cannot even insult the photographer, he simply gives up the picture. The effect on the reader is pathos — laughter turns to sympathy in a single sentence.
questions.explanation: The ending works because it reverses the sketch's tone: after pages of comedy, one image of weeping reveals the real injury. The explanation should connect the tears to the theme (self-acceptance refused) and to the narrator's character (polite, vulnerable, honest).
questions.commonMistake: Calling the ending 'unexpected' without explaining what it means — the mark is for interpretation, not surprise.

questions.prompt: Where and when is the sketch set? What details place it in its period?
questions.answer: The sketch is set in a photographer's waiting room and studio in the early twentieth century. The period is suggested rather than stated: formal studio photography of the era, the mention of a Ladies Companion annual for 1912, and the photographer's hand-retouching of the proof all belong to the age before instant snapshots and digital cameras.
questions.explanation: The question wants the two locations (waiting room and studio) plus period evidence. Leacock never names a city, so answers should not invent one — the setting is deliberately ordinary and general.
questions.commonMistake: Inventing a city or country: the text gives none, and unsupported specifics lose marks.

questions.prompt: 'The sketch is funny until it is not.' Discuss whether you agree, using the ending of the sketch in your answer.
questions.answer: There is a strong case for the statement. For most of its length the sketch is comic: the narrator's polite protests, the photographer's solemn pronouncements, and the catalogue of alterations — eyes, eyebrows, mouth, ears — all invite laughter at the absurdity of treating a face as a repair job. But the final image of the narrator leaving in tears changes the value of everything before it: we realise that his good humour was a way of enduring an insult, and that the 'improvement' he was offered amounted to being told he was unacceptable. The comedy does not disappear; it becomes uncomfortable, because the reader is now laughing at something that genuinely wounded a gentle man. One may argue the opposite — that the ending is itself comic in its exaggeration — but Leacock gives the tears no comic tag, which suggests he intends sympathy to have the last word.
questions.explanation: This is a discuss question: state a judgement, argue it with evidence from both the comic incidents and the ending, and acknowledge the counter-reading. The strongest answers notice that the ending does not cancel the humour but revalues it.
questions.commonMistake: Only summarising the funny moments — a discussion must take a position and defend it with the ending.

questions.prompt: If the narrator had his own portrait studio, how would he treat a customer? Answer as if describing the opposite of the photographer's behaviour, and explain what your answer reveals about the sketch's values.
questions.answer: In the opposite of this studio, the customer's wishes would come first: the narrator would ask how the sitter wants to be seen, arrange the lighting to flatter without falsifying, and hand over a photograph the sitter recognises as themselves. Alterations would be offered, never imposed, and no feature would be described as wrong. The sketch's values become clear in this reversal: it prizes truth over flattery, consent over expert authority, and acceptance over 'improvement'. The narrator's imagined studio is not anti-art — it simply insists that a portrait belongs to the person in it, which is exactly the principle the photographer ignored and exactly why the narrator wept.
questions.explanation: A hypothetical question of this kind tests whether you can state a work's values by inverting its conflict. Each feature of the imagined studio should answer a specific wrong in the original: consent answers presumption, recognition answers retouching, the customer's wish answers the expert's opinion.
questions.commonMistake: Writing a general essay on good customer service — every point must be tied back to what happens in Leacock's sketch.
